newsitem.title: JAPAN: Mighty yen falls victim to Asian currency crisis.
newsitem.headline: Mighty yen falls victim to Asian currency crisis.

text.p: The Japanese yen, once the safe-haven currency of Asia, has finally fallen victim to the currency crisis sweeping the region, traders said on Friday.

Until now, currency sell-offs in the region had sparked yen buying as the investors fled to the stability of the yen as Asian nations, such as Thailand, fought a losing battle with currency speculators.

But traders said that given the magnitude of the economic and financial ties between Japan and other Asian nations and the poor investment climate in Japan, continued turmoil in Asia is likely to trigger yen sales against the U.S. dollar.

"Given Japan's strong economic link with Asia, further deterioration in the situation will also harm Japan and is likely to cause yen sales," said Hokuto Nakano, manager of the international treasury department at the Industrial Bank of Japan.
"Money fleeing from Asian nations are mainly going to the United States where the performance of the economy and financial markets is far better than Japan," he added.
The U.S. dollar rose as high as around 118.44 yen in Asia on Friday, after ending at around 117.80 yen in New York.

On Thursday, Indonesia's central bank said it was lifting the intervention band with immediate effect, virtually making the rupiah a freely-floating currency -- the latest among Asian nations since Thailand's similar announcement on July 2.
The Indonesian rupiah settled about five percent down on the day against the U.S. dollar.
Singapore and Malaysia are also apparently allowing the value of their currencies to weaken in a bid to maintain a competitive edge over exports.
"We are seeing a similar image of the period during the Mexican currency crisis," said IBJ's Nakano.
When the Mexican currency crisis erupted in 1995, the U.S. dollar was sold heavily against the yen because of the United States' strong link with the Mexican economy.

Currency dealers sold off the U.S. dollar heavily to below 100 yen as they thought that the Mexican's problem would affect the NAFTA (North American Free Trade Agreement) regime and the U.S. dollar's credibility as well.
The International Monetary Fund put together a $40 billion rescue package for ailing Mexico, led by the United States.
Similarly, Japan pledged on Monday to take a fourth of the burden on a global $16 billion bailout scheme for Thailand to ease its credit crunch and prevent a regional chain reaction.

Major Japanese commercial banks are also heavily exposed to Asian nations as they looked to Asia as the best place to lend money since the early 1990s in the face of moribund demand for funds at home. There were also around 10,000 subsidiaries of Japanese companies in Asia at the end of 1996.
Mikio Yasutake, foreign exchange and treasury division manager at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, said a capital flight into the yen --as seen after the baht flotation-- will be limited.
"Rather, yen sales are outstanding in light of Japan's linkage with other Asia nations," he said.
"If Japan's exports to Asian nations fall as a result of the economic slump there, there is a question of how Japan will replace that," he added.
Amid the sluggish domestic demand at home and tight fiscal policy, Japan's economic recovery is mainly led by exports.
Japan is mainly exporting capital goods to Asian nations so that they can use them to complete building products and export them elsewhere, such as the United States.

Japanese companies have rushed to Asian nations to localise their production since the mid-1980s after a dramatic rise in the yen and these massive direct investments contributed to the growth of the so-called Asian Tiger economies.
"There is no sign at all that Asian currencies are going back to their previous levels," IBJ's Nakano said.
"But if such regional jitters result in pushing the dollar up to 120 yen, the (Japanese) monetary authorities could start showing concerns about such movements," he added.
